issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically to stop thinking about a single mugging/robbery is clinically possible but is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile because there are no memory/intrusion items, no trigger-linked re-experiencing pattern, and the formulation leaves Triggers and Memory inactive. This strategy addresses a symptom pattern not otherwise represented in the selected items.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is not impossible, but for a mugging/robbery it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile. The other items emphasize hyperarousal, threat sensitivity, institutional betrayal, and numbing; this culturally/community-focused appraisal is not clearly linked to those features or to the formulation's active appraisal-threat-strategy loop, making it the least coherent appraisal item in this set.

vignette:
Elena had always moved through the city with the brisk certainty of someone who knew her value and her route. At fifty-three, she was a senior stock broker on a high-stakes trading floor, accustomed to chaos that was controlled, to numbers that obeyed rules. That Tuesday evening last September, however, broke every rule. She had stayed later than usual to close out a volatile position. When she finally left the office, her usual path to the subway took her through a short pedestrian tunnel beneath the financial district. She had used it hundreds of times. That night, a man appeared from behind a pillar, pressed a blade against her ribs, and demanded her bag, her watch, her phone. Elena froze. She did not scream. She did not run. She handed over everything, performing compliance so absolute that the man seemed almost bored. He disappeared into the stairwell. She stood there for several minutes, unable to move, before she realised she had no way to call anyone. When she finally reached the street and flagged down a patrol car, the officers took a report but told her that without a description or a camera, there was little they could do. The case was closed within a week. The institution that should have protected her had shrugged.

That night, Elena began to notice that ordinary sounds made her jump—the click of a light switch, the clatter of her husband settling into bed. She started sleeping with the hallway light on, then with a chair wedged under the bedroom door. Within a month, she had developed a private ritual: every time she walked into a new room, she had to count to seven under her breath before she could sit down. If she was interrupted mid-count, she had to start over. She knew it made no sense, but she could not stop—the fear that something terrible would happen if she broke the count was too strong. At work, she found herself scanning the trading floor constantly, her eyes darting from doorway to doorway, tracking every sudden movement. When a colleague reached across her desk without warning, her whole body locked into a rigid, eager-to-please posture—she would apologise even when nothing was wrong, agree to any request, smile too quickly. She hated herself for it, but the alternative—saying no, standing her ground—felt like an invitation to violence. The world had shown her its true shape: unpredictable, dangerous, indifferent to her safety.

Elena had always been a woman who felt things intensely, but now she noticed a dullness creeping in. She would sit through dinner with her husband and feel nothing—not irritation, not affection, just a thick emptiness. When he tried to hold her hand, she felt disconnected from the gesture, as if it belonged to someone else’s life. She began to cancel their evening walks, claiming exhaustion, because the mere sight of someone approaching from behind made her chest tighten with a rush of fear and anger so sharp it surprised her. She was angry at the man who had taken her things, at the police who had dismissed her, at herself for having felt safe in the first place. But expressing any of that felt impossible; instead, she would go silent and compliant, nodding along, while inside a loop of replays ran: the blade, the cold, her own obedience.

What finally brought Elena to seek help was a moment on the subway platform. A young man in a hooded sweatshirt shifted his weight suddenly, reaching into his pocket, and Elena dropped her coffee, flinched so hard that she nearly fell onto the tracks. Passengers stared. She felt a shame so acute it burned. That night, she told her husband she could not keep living this way—jumping at shadows, counting in her head, feeling dead behind a mask of pleasantness. She was not sure what she hoped a therapist could do. Part of her was certain that no amount of talking could make the world safe, that the institutions had already failed and would fail again. But the numbness had become unbearable, and that small, terrified part of her that still remembered the city as a place of opportunity—not a hunting ground—wanted, somehow, to believe otherwise.
